$comment: Shared state for ONE work-graph run. Lives at .graph/runs/<run-id>/state.json. Every node reads this on start and appends to its OWN key on finish - the builder writes its own builders.<slice> key, including the branch it worked on. Never rewrite another node's key. Every node key carries written_by, naming the node that wrote it: that is the ONLY record of authorship this file has, and without it 'never rewrite another node's key' is unverifiable - an orchestrator hand-writing all six keys is indistinguishable from six nodes doing their jobs. verify-state.py --audit checks it. This file is the edge: it is how context crosses between agents that cannot see each other.

decisions_for_gate.topic: Which stored host the controller loads (item 1; amends the G5 text that the A1 UI shows the first host)
decisions_for_gate.recommend: The largest paired_at; a tie goes to the later index entry. paired_at already exists in every record (store.ts:14, set at controller.ts:270), so no schema change and no migration. A re-pair of an existing id updates its paired_at in place, so the host paired last is always the one loaded. It also fixes the s3-review edge where a transiently hidden host A came back ahead of a just-paired B. Forget still returns to unpaired until the next start (see NOT DOING).
alternatives: Last connected: a new last_connected_at field written on every goLive; a record schema change and a SecureStore write per connect. Better if two live desktops are normal; not needed for the one-host A1 UI.
Keep the first host (status quo): a reinstalled desktop shows Not paired after every restart until Forget.

decisions_for_gate.topic: Cancel during a re-pair of the same host id (item 3; closes a G6 violation)
decisions_for_gate.recommend: Before saveHost, read the stored record with that host_id through listHosts (HostStore unchanged). On a cancel after the save: restore it with saveHost(previous); if there was none, forgetHost(new id) as today; if the lookup threw, do neither. A failed restore deletes nothing: the store then holds the new record, which the desktop has confirmed and which works, while memory keeps the old one until restart. The desktop keeps a confirmed client entry either way (inherent, already accepted in A1). This also covers re-pairing a stored host that is not the current one, which a this.record snapshot would miss.
alternatives: Null this.record and forget the id (the other reviewer suggestion): loses the old keys, which is the G6 violation itself.
Check pairCancelled before saveHost only: shrinks the window, but a Cancel during the save still lands after the overwrite.
Add getHost to HostStore: one more interface method and a provider edit for the same result.

decisions_for_gate.recommend: Salvage, no UI copy. A value that is not a JSON array of host ids is read as the distinct 32-hex ids found in its text; array entries that are not host ids are dropped; the next save or forget rewrites a clean array. An id with no record is already harmless (skipped). This never blocks Pair or Forget, needs no new screen, and recovers every id whose text survived. What is lost: a value with no recognisable id reads as empty and its records stay unreachable, because SecureStore cannot enumerate keys. A throwing read stays strict on write paths, as today.
alternatives: Strict: refuse to write over a present but unparseable index, plus a Reset paired desktops action. Needs a new controller method (a provider API change), a screen element and copy, for example: 'Orchestra cannot read its list of paired desktops on this phone. Reset it, then pair again. [Reset]'. Blocks Pair and Forget until the user acts.
Status quo and document it: the next save orphans every other record and its secret.

decisions_for_gate.recommend: One message for PairAuthFailed that names both causes: 'This code did not work with the desktop at that address, or the connection dropped. Show a new code on the desktop and scan it again.' decisions_for_gate.topic: RN onerror and onclose (the item 5 check) and the fix it turns up
decisions_for_gate.recommend: Include in s3. Read from RN 0.86.3 source, not run on a device: on Android every failure, a host drop or a network drop alike, arrives as a bare error Event with no message followed by a close with code 1006 and reason = the OkHttp exception text (WebSocket.js:273-286, WebSocketModule.kt:170-172 and 330-338). So the close code never separates the causes and the reason text is an exception message, not a contract; nothing new keys off it. But client.ts:248-252 fails at once in opening with errorText empty (the RN error event has no message), so the close that carries the 404 reason is ignored and a used or closed code at /pair shows Unreachable on a device, not PairWindowClosed (G6 (1)). The fix lets onclose do the mapping in every phase; the existing tests stay green and a new RN-shaped test pins it.
alternatives: Leave it and add an owner device check for the 404 path: G6 (1) stays broken on Android until then.
Defer to a separate follow-up run: same code, same files as s3.

s1.$comment: RE-REVIEWS NEST, and this is the rule every reader follows. The TOP LEVEL of reviews.<slice> IS attempt 1. A re-review writes attempt_2, then attempt_3, and so on, each with the same fields as the top level. Every attempt SURVIVES PERMANENTLY - history is never overwritten, flattened, or migrated up. The LATEST attempt supplies the verdict: that is what close-run.py, brief.py and verify-state.py resolve through, and what fleetview's finalVerdict() has always shown. `ever_rejected` - did ANY attempt REJECT - is DISPLAY ONLY, forever, so a rejection stays visible after it is fixed; it must never gate anything, or the fleet stops being able to loop. NO NODE MAY REWRITE AN EARLIER ATTEMPT: a second reviewer writes its own attempt_N and leaves the ones before it alone, top-level verdict included - relocating that verdict would destroy the history the board keeps and leave a key stamped written_by:reviewer with someone else as its real author. The KEY INDEX numbers an attempt, not the `attempt` field inside it; the field is display. An EMPTY attempt_N is not a re-review, it is a key nobody wrote - write the whole attempt or none of it. The walk STOPS AT THE FIRST GAP, so an attempt_3 with no attempt_2 is ignored and the earlier verdict stands: A GAP IS MALFORMED AND NO NODE MAY LEAVE ONE. Write the next UNUSED N and never skip - a mis-numbered re-review is not reported anywhere, it is simply unread, and a REJECT nobody reads is a REJECT nobody acts on. The cap is attempt_9, matching fleetview's `for (i = 2; i < 10; i++)` exactly so the two readers cannot disagree; attempt_10 and beyond is reported loudly and resolved by nobody.

findings.title: The 404 match is an unanchored substring, and s3 makes it live on a device
findings.detail: closedBy tests reason.includes('404'). Before s3 this could not happen on Android, because onerror failed first with an empty errorText. Now it runs on the OkHttp exception text. In OkHttp 4.9.2 (the RN pin, gradle/libs.versions.toml:37), a refused connect is rewrapped as 'Failed to connect to /<ip>:<port>'. On /pair, a desktop on a configured port containing 404 (4040, 14040, 40400-40499, ...) that refuses the connection shows PairWindowClosed ('code already used') instead of Unreachable. Reproduced with a scratch test: reason 'Failed to connect to /1.2.3.4:4040' -> PairWindowClosed. IPv4 octets cannot form 404. The default port 47800 is unaffected and no key is touched, so this is a wrong message, not a G6 key breach. The F5 claim that refused text 'lacks 404' holds only for such ports. Suggested follow-up: match /but was '404 / or / 404 /.

findings.title: openMs < OkHttp connectTimeout is now load-bearing
findings.detail: A SocketTimeoutException from Android libcore is not rewrapped by OkHttp, and its text carries the local ephemeral port ('... from /x (port 40412) after 10000ms'). It never reaches closedBy only because openMs (5 s) fires before WebSocketModule's 10 s connectTimeout. Raising openMs to 10 s or more would let a random local port containing 404 misclassify. Worth a comment.

findings.issue: The lookup's throw branch (previous=undefined, leave new record) is unreachable with the real store: listHosts reads the index and records non-strict and turns any SecureStore throw into absent. Input: re-pair stored host X, getItemAsync throws transiently during the lookup, Cancel lands during the save -> previous=null -> forgetHost(X) deletes X's record and index entry. Not a regression (pre-slice always forgot) and the plan mandated listHosts with HostStore unchanged, so not a blocker; the F2 third branch only works against a fake store. A fix would need a strict lookup (interface change).

listHosts is not run through the store queue, so a forgetHost already queued for the same id (for example the void forget at :489 after revoked) can still be pending when the lookup reads the old record; a Cancel after the save then restores the record that was just forgotten. It heals itself (the next connect is revoked again and deleted) and needs a re-pair within milliseconds of the forget.

There is now an await (the lookup) between welcome and saveHost with no epoch check after it, so a dispose during the lookup still saves the new record and keeps it. The same was already true for a dispose during the save, and the desktop has confirmed the key, so the behaviour is consistent with what A1 shipped.

'a failed restore deletes nothing' checks that forgotten is [] and that saveHost was called twice, but not the state afterwards: the store keeps the new record while memory keeps the old one until the next start, as F2 accepts. No test covers a listHosts that throws, which the plan's 9-test list did not ask for.

The deviation (the stored host is added after start) hides no user path. The cancel branch never reads this.record, so with a current host A the only difference is that finish() resumes A. The ProtocolError comes from the fake host, which serves vectors only for the kk host id; it is not something a user can reach.

The salvage can capture a 32-hex run that is not a host id, for example one with an uppercase or non-hex neighbour. Such an id has no record, so listHosts skips it and it stays in the index as a harmless entry. No secret can be captured: the client secret and the host key are 64 hex, which the lookarounds reject.
